_readme: Every string, image path, icon name and weave token the `marlowe` template renders. Marlowe.jsx contains no copy of its own, so rebranding this house, translating it, or pointing it at real photography is an edit to this file and a rebuild. `icon` values are lucide-react export names resolved through the ICONS table in the JSX; `weave` and `mark` values resolve through WEAVES and MARKS. A name missing from any of those tables renders nothing rather than throwing, so a typo here degrades instead of white-screening the page. Every `image`, `src` and `video` key may be null: the section falls back to a drawn plate, which is how this template ships. There is no tailoring photography in this repo and nothing may be hotlinked, so the cloth is drawn in CSS rather than shot — see the header comment in Marlowe.jsx. Setting any of these keys to a real path swaps the drawing for the photograph with no code change.

brand.name: Marlowe & Hale
brand.documentTitle: Marlowe & Hale — Bespoke Tailors, Savile Row

hero.heading: A coat cut for one man only
hero.body: Eighty-two hours of hand work, four fittings, and a paper pattern kept for life. We have made in this room since 1868, and we have never made the same coat twice.

register: By appointment to the Household Division
The Rake — House of the Year
Permanent Style — Best of British Tailoring
Founding member, Savile Row Bespoke Association
Financial Times — How to Spend It

house.statement: We are cutters before we are anything else. Everything this house does begins on the board with a length of cloth and a piece of chalk.
body: Josiah Marlowe took the lease on No. 14 in 1868 with one cutting board and a debt to his former master. Thomas Hale joined him nine years later, and the partnership has outlasted six monarchs, two fires and one direct hit in 1941 that took the roof but not the pattern room.

Those patterns are the house. Eleven thousand four hundred of them, each cut to one man, filed by hand, and kept whether he returns next season or in thirty years. A grandson can order his grandfather's coat and we will cut it from the same paper.

before.heading: Three and a half metres of cloth

steps.title: The consultation
steps.body: An hour in the front room. What you need the coat to do, where you will wear it, and what you already own that works. No measuring yet.

steps.title: Measure and cloth
steps.body: Thirty-one measurements taken by the cutter who will cut you. The cloth is chosen from the mill books in the same sitting, because the cloth decides the cut.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body: Your pattern is drafted in brown paper and cut by hand. It is yours in perpetuity and it never leaves this building.

steps.title: The baste fitting
steps.body: The coat comes to you in white basting thread, unfinished and deliberately wrong in places, so the cutter can see what the paper could not tell him.

steps.title: The forward fitting
steps.body: Canvas in, sleeves on, collar set. This is the fitting where the coat stops being an idea. Most commissions need one; some need two.

steps.title: Delivery
steps.body: Finished, pressed, and your pattern filed. We keep a note of the cloth so the trousers can be repeated in five years when the coat still has life in it.

items.name: The Fourteen
items.body: The house coat. Two buttons, soft shoulder, a light canvas and a slightly extended waist. Named for the door.
items.alt: The Fourteen, a two-button single-breasted coat

items.name: The Marlowe
items.body: Josiah's own cut, drafted in 1871 and unchanged since. Higher gorge, roped shoulder, a firmer chest. Worn by men who stand for a living.
items.alt: The Marlowe, a structured single-breasted coat

items.name: The Hale
items.body: Double-breasted, six on two, with a peak lapel cut long. The most formal thing we make that is not black tie.
items.alt: The Hale, a six-on-two double-breasted coat

items.name: The Evening
items.body: Dinner jacket, shawl or peak, faced in silk from Macclesfield. Made once and worn for thirty years, which is the correct way round.
items.alt: The Evening, a shawl-collar dinner jacket

makers.name: Edith Rowan
makers.body: Learned under the last of the Hales. Cuts every first pattern in the house and will not let a coat leave until the balance is right, which is why some of them are late.

makers.name: Samuel Achebe
makers.body: Makes the body and the canvas. Everything that gives a coat its shape happens under his hands, and none of it is visible when it is finished.

makers.name: Nadia Sørensen
makers.body: Trousers are the harder half and the one nobody praises. Hers hang from the waistband without a wrinkle, which is the whole art.

makers.name: Rory Callan
makers.body: Buttonholes, edges, linings, and every stitch that shows. The youngest bench in the room and the one with the steadiest hand.

cloth.heading: Nine hundred books, six mills
cloth.note: Weights in ounces per yard. We will cut anything you bring us, but these are the cloths we know the behaviour of.

swatches.name: Lovat Herringbone
swatches.caption: The house tweed. Cut for country coats and the only cloth we will make an unstructured jacket in.

swatches.name: City Chalkstripe
swatches.caption: Worsted flannel, chalked at seven-eighths of an inch. The stripe is soft enough to read as texture across a room.

swatches.name: Midnight Birdseye
swatches.caption: Navy so dark it reads black under electric light and navy in daylight. The most useful cloth in the book.

swatches.name: Border Glen Check
swatches.caption: A quiet check with a faint claret overcheck. Loud enough to notice, quiet enough to wear twice a week.

swatches.name: Summer Hopsack
swatches.caption: An open basket weave that breathes. The only thing we recommend for a coat that has to survive August.

swatches.name: Evening Barathea
swatches.caption: The correct cloth for a dinner jacket and the reason a good one does not shine under a flash.

items.title: A shooting coat for a Perthshire estate
items.body: Lovat herringbone at 13oz, bellows pockets, an action back, and a lining the client chose to match his dogs. Made to be soaked and to dry flat.

items.title: A first suit, for a call to the Bar
items.body: Midnight birdseye, the Marlowe cut, and his grandfather's pattern taken out of the file for the trouser rise. Both men were measured in this room forty-one years apart.

items.title: A dinner jacket for a fiftieth
items.body: Barathea, shawl collar faced in Ellisfield silk, and one covered button. He asked for it to look like 1962 without looking like a costume.

items.title: A covert coat, remade from a 1974 pattern
items.body: The original came in with the lining gone and the cloth still sound. We cut a new one from the same pattern and four rows of stitching at the hem, as it was.

workshop.heading: Three floors, one of them below the pavement
workshop.body: The shop is the smallest part of this building. Above it is the cutting room, above that the workroom, and beneath the pavement the pattern store, which is the only room with a lock on it.

points.title: The board
points.body: Nine feet of Honduras mahogany, laid in 1868 and never replaced. Every pattern this house has ever cut was cut on it.

points.title: The pattern store
points.body: Eleven thousand four hundred patterns in brown paper, filed by name. Nothing is thrown away, including the patterns of men long dead.

points.title: The books
points.body: Nine hundred cloth books from six mills, kept in date order. The oldest still in use was bound in 1957 and half of it can still be woven.

answers.heading: What people ask before the first appointment

items.question: How long does a commission take?
answer: Twenty to twenty-four weeks for a first coat, and about sixteen for anything after that, because the pattern already exists.
We will not rush a first commission. The baste fitting has to be looked at with fresh eyes a week later, and that week is not padding.

items.question: What does it cost, and what changes the price?
answer: A two-piece begins at £5,400 and the cloth moves it from there. A 9oz hopsack and a 13oz tweed are not the same money, and neither are six buttonholes and twelve.
The price we quote at the second appointment is the price on delivery. Fittings are not charged for, however many are needed.

items.question: How many fittings will I need?
answer: Three is normal for a first commission: baste, forward, and a final try-on at delivery. Some figures need a fourth and we would rather do it than not.
Fittings are forty-five minutes and we ask that you come in the shoes you will wear with the suit.

items.question: Do you travel?
answer: Twice a year to New York and Hong Kong, and once to Zurich. Dates go to the order book first and to the register on this page after that.
A first commission is better begun here, because a first pattern wants a second pair of eyes on the board.

items.question: Can I bring my own cloth?
answer: Yes, and we will tell you honestly if it will not do what you want. Three and a half metres for a two-piece, four and a quarter with a waistcoat.
Cloth we have not woven with before is cut at the client's risk, which we will say once and not labour.

items.question: Do you alter what you have made?
answer: For as long as the coat exists and whoever is wearing it. Bodies change and a bespoke coat has the inlays to follow them, which is most of the point of one.
Alterations to our own work are not charged for in the first two years.

clients.heading: Letters kept in the order book

items.quote: I came in for a suit for a funeral and left having been talked out of it. They made me something I could wear afterwards instead, which is not what a shop does.
items.name: H. Ashworth-Bell

items.quote: The coat is fourteen years old. It has been altered three times, relined once, and it still fits better than anything I have bought since.
items.name: Dr. Priya Raghunathan

items.quote: My father was measured on that board and so was I. When I brought my son in, Edith found the 1983 pattern in under a minute and did not make a performance of it.
items.name: James Okonkwo-Hart

fitting.heading: The first appointment is an hour and costs nothing
fitting.body: Tell us roughly what you are after and when you can come. We will write back within two working days with a time, and with the cloth books already out if you have named something.

newsletter.title: The Register
newsletter.body: Travelling dates and new cloth, four times a year. Nothing else.
